title: 🔬 Handwritten semiconductor notes: detailed reading and technical connections

paras: This chapter reads the latest 15 pages individually rather than treating them as a single topic. Each entry separates source topics from editorial elaboration/correction . Earlier source pages remain preserved in the source gallery, but are not falsely marked as individually audited.

Source observation = a careful topical reading of the photographed page, not a certified verbatim transcription. Technical expansion = independently written explanation and correction. Cross-links = related chapters. Where handwriting is faint or ambiguous, use the original photograph as authoritative.
Communication/interface chips: Wi-Fi and Bluetooth modems, display drivers; programmable logic: FPGA.

A wireless modem integrates baseband/control functions, but radio front-end, antenna and host interface may be separate. Display drivers convert pixel/control data into electrical drive signals. FPGA is reconfigurable digital hardware rather than a generic blank chip.
Related chapters: C09 · C11
Analog amplifiers, filters, oscillators; digital logic gates, combinational and sequential circuits; mixed-signal ADC/DAC; power circuits.

Analog signals are continuous in amplitude, while digital circuits interpret voltage ranges as logic states. Combinational logic depends on present inputs; sequential logic depends on state and clock/event history. ADCs sample and quantize; DACs reconstruct analog levels. Power circuits convert/regulate energy, not merely heavy current.
Related chapters: C08 · C10
Logic/processing CPU GPU MCU ASIC; memory DRAM SRAM NAND EEPROM; PMIC voltage and battery management; RF/Ethernet/display/audio; linear and timer chips.

Classify by function, not packaging: CPU and GPU may share a SoC; an MCU includes CPU and peripherals; ASIC describes custom-purpose implementation. DRAM is volatile, NAND is persistent, EEPROM supports small rewritable nonvolatile storage. PMIC includes rails, sequencing and protection.
Related chapters: C08 · C09 · C10
Micro standalone trackers/headphones: MCU, SRAM, firmware storage, Bluetooth RF, battery chips. Personal devices: CPU/SoC, DRAM, NAND, modem, display driver, audio codec.

A tracker can be an SoC with embedded flash and radio rather than multiple separate ICs. ARM is an ISA family, not itself a microcontroller. Smartphone SoCs combine application CPU, GPU, NPU and peripherals, often with separate RF/power components.
Related chapters: C09 · C10 · C11

blocks.h2: Edge, data center and cloud devices
paras: Edge: traffic lights, autonomous vehicles, FPGAs, NPUs, ECC RAM and rugged PMICs. Data center: server blades, CPUs/GPUs, DDR5, NVMe and smart NICs.

Safety-critical edge controllers require deterministic behavior, watchdogs and fail-safe design; an FPGA is not required for every edge system. ECC detects/corrects certain memory errors. SmartNIC/DPU offloads networking/storage/security tasks but does not replace the host CPU.
Related chapters: C10 · C11
IBM Z mainframes, HBM, interconnect switching, distributed clusters and supercomputers.

Mainframes emphasize resilient transaction processing, I/O, partitioning and availability; HPC systems emphasize parallel numerical throughput. HBM is used in many accelerators but is not the defining memory for all mainframes. Cluster interconnects differ from ordinary Ethernet depending on design.
Related chapters: C09 · C10 · C11

CPU runs OS/applications; GPU accelerates graphics/AI; MCU firmware; NPU neural workloads; ASIC fixed logic; FPGA reconfigurable. SRAM/DRAM/ROM/flash/GDDR/HBM. PCIe USB Ethernet SATA NVMe I²C SPI Wi-Fi BLE RF front-end NFC GPS.

PCIe/USB/I²C/SPI are buses/interconnects, Ethernet and Wi-Fi are network families, NVMe is a storage command protocol, and SATA is a storage interface. NFC and GNSS/GPS have distinct communication/positioning roles. An FPGA configuration is hardware logic, not just editable software.
Related chapters: C09 · C10 · C11
CPUs GPUs MCUs NPUs FPGAs ASICs; single-chip SoC, motherboard integration, chip functions for personal/cloud/distributed computing.

SoC refers to integration of multiple functional blocks on one die, not necessarily all device components. A motherboard contains packages, buses and connectors; a module may contain several chips. CISC/RISC and ASIC/FPGA are independent classification axes.
Related chapters: C09 · C10
SRAM cache L1/L2/L3; DRAM DDR4/DDR5 LPDDR; HBM 3D stacks; NAND SSDs; EEPROM/NOR firmware; bus communication and DMA.

SRAM commonly implements cache but cache is a managed hierarchy, not just a chip. DRAM requires refresh. HBM stacks memory dies with high bandwidth. NAND is erased in blocks and programmed in pages; SSD controller manages wear-leveling and flash translation. EEPROM and NOR differ in access/erase granularity. DMA transfers data without CPU copying every byte, but CPU/software still configures it.
Related chapters: C10 · C11
PMIC/VRM power conversion; embedded controller; cache controller; integrated memory controller; NVMe/USB storage controllers; ports and buses.

A VRM supplies regulated voltage; PMIC may sequence rails and handle charging. Cache controllers track tags/coherence; memory controllers schedule DRAM commands; SSD controllers manage NAND. A USB port is a connector/transport endpoint, not inherently master/slave. Ethernet is switched packet networking, not merely peer-to-peer.
Related chapters: C08 · C10 · C11
CPU GPU MCU NPU SoC ASIC DSP FPGA; processing as brain, memory as storage, communications as messenger, PMIC as fuel system, timer as synchronization.

Analogy is pedagogical, not literal: devices can operate autonomously and use DMA/interrupts. A GPU is itself a processor; a SoC is a package of subsystems; DSP targets signal operations; an ASIC may contain a CPU. Clocks synchronize circuitry while OS schedulers decide which software task runs.
Related chapters: C09 · C10
Processing executes software; memory holds active/persistent data; power distributes regulated rails; communication interfaces connect systems; linear/timer handles analog and clock signals.

Not every digital device uses five physically separate chips; integrated SoCs collapse several families, while some analog devices need no programmable processor. ROM and NAND differ; RF transceivers, MACs and PHYs occupy different protocol layers.
Related chapters: C08 · C09 · C10
RISC/CISC, ARM/x86-64, application-specific ASIC, reconfigurable FPGA, MCU for simpler devices; general-purpose CPU/SoC for complex devices.

ISA (ARM, x86, RISC-V) differs from microarchitecture and implementation substrate (ASIC/FPGA). RISC does not guarantee low power and CISC does not guarantee performance. ASIC fixed-function hardware can include programmable embedded cores; FPGA logic can implement CPUs.
Related chapters: C09

blocks.h2: RISC, CISC, ASIC and FPGA deployment
paras: Battery-focused RISC, high-performance CISC, ASIC networking/embedded, FPGA telecom/aerospace/hardware development.

These are tendencies, not strict mappings: Arm servers are high performance; x86 laptops can be power efficient; ASICs are used widely for high-volume acceleration; FPGAs can be production deployed in networks. Compare workloads, software ecosystem, latency, power and unit economics.
Related chapters: C09 · C11
Wireless RF front-end, USB device/tracking, satellite modem; wired optical transceiver, PCIe switch, Thunderbolt controller; network chip ASIC, PHY, flash, NIC, VLAN.

RF front-end conditions radio signals; baseband/modem processes protocol waveforms. Optical transceiver converts electrical/optical signals; a PCIe switch routes PCIe transactions; a network switch ASIC forwards Ethernet frames. PHY handles physical-layer signaling; NIC joins host memory/driver to a link. VLAN is a logical segmentation mechanism implemented in switch/NIC software/hardware, not a separate chip.
Related chapters: C10 · C11

blocks.h2: From a sensor to a cloud dashboard
paras: Physical event → sensor transducer → analog filter/amplifier → ADC (if needed) → MCU peripheral registers → firmware driver → local buffer in SRAM → Wi-Fi/BLE/cellular controller → RF front end and antenna → access point/base station → Ethernet/IP routers → cloud NIC → Linux driver → TCP/TLS service → database → dashboard.

Every edge has a different responsibility: conversion, conditioning, sampling, device access, buffering, framing, modulation, packet forwarding, kernel delivery, transport security and application processing. A digital sensor can combine several early stages; BLE may relay through a phone instead of direct Internet access.

blocks.h2: From an NVMe file to a CPU instruction
paras: NAND cells → SSD controller error correction/flash translation → NVMe command completion → PCIe transactions → DMA into DRAM → OS page cache/filesystem → virtual memory mapping → CPU cache hierarchy → instruction/data access. The CPU orchestrates through software and controllers, but dedicated hardware performs many transfers.

Optical module/copper PHY → Ethernet MAC in NIC → RX descriptor ring → DMA to RAM → interrupt moderation/NAPI polling → Linux driver → network stack and firewall → socket → application. Outbound packets traverse the inverse stages; a SmartNIC or DPU can offload selected work.
